In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[Edo period]]. During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[Tsuno Station]] on the [[JR Kyushu]] [[Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. It is also claimed that [[Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[Edo period]]. During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commons Category-inline}} *{{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} ==Notes== {{reflist}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Miyazaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Kokuhei Shōsha]] [[Category:Shikinai Shosha]] [[Category:Hyūga Province]] }} [[en:Tsuno Shrine]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] {{Commons category|Tsuno-jinja}} [[fr:Tsuno-jinja]] [[ja:都農神社]] [[Category:Pages with simple english wikipedia interwikis]][[simple:Tsuno Shrine]] [[zh:都農神社]] {{wikidata link|Q3541675}} [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] == Accidentally Overwritten Content == [[sn:commons:Category:Tsuno-jinja]][[en:Tsuno Shrine]][[fr:Tsuno-jinja]][[ja:都農神社]][[simple:Tsuno Shrine]][[zh:都農神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q3541675]] Wikidata name: Tsuno Shrine [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:09, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Miyazaki Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Tsuno Shrine
都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[:en:Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[:en:Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[:en:Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[:en:Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[:en:Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[:en:Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[:en:Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[:en:Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. 都農神社 | image = File:Tsuno Shrine 2009 001.JPG | caption = Tsuno Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Miyazaki Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|32.263056|N|131.558611|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno-cho, Koyo-gun, Miyazaki-ken 502-0071 Japan | website = {{Official|1=https://tunojinjya6.webnode.jp}} | architecture_style = | festival = December 5 | leadership = | location = {{ill|Tsuno|WD=Q1205974}} }} [[File:Tsuno-jinja minamitorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]] {{nihongo|'''Tsuno Shrine''' |都農神社|Tsuno Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in the Kawakita neighborhood of the town of [[:en:Tsuno, Miyazaki|Tsuno]], [[:en:Miyazaki Prefecture|Miyazaki Prefecture]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{Cite web |last=TOKYO |first=COPYRIGHT © KYUSHU × |title=Tsuno Shrine {{!}} KYUSHU x TOKYO (JAPAN) |url=https://www.kyushuandtokyo.org/spot_203/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=www.kyushuandtokyo.org |language=en}} It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the former [[:en:Hyūga Province|Hyūga Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on December 5.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Tsuno Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Ōkuninushi]]'''| 大己貴命 |}} head of the ''kunitsukami'', the gods of the earth, and the original ruler of the terrestrial world,{{Cite web |last=公益財団法人宮崎県観光協会・宮崎県 |title=都農神社 |url=https://www.kanko-miyazaki.jp/tsuno/kanko/12012.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=【公式】みやざき観光情報「旬ナビ」 |language=ja}} ==History== The foundation of Tsuno Shrine is unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded six years before [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]]'s accession to the throne, when the Emperor departed Hyūga on his expedition to conquer the east. It is also claimed that [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] worshipped at this location for the safety of her fleet during her conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and said that the first time that the shrine was built was after the Empress's triumphant return. In addition to the ruins dating back to the [[Jōmon period]], the Tsuno area is home to more than 20 [[kofun|Kofun]]s (the [[Tsuno Kofun Cluster]]), and pottery and [[:en:Stone tool|Stone tool]]s have been excavated near the site of the shrine. In 837 the shrine was promoted to a government shrine, and in 843 was awarded Junior Fifth Rank, per the "[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]"). In 858, it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank per the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', it is one of only four shrines listed for Hyūga Province, and at that time it was the largest shrine in Hyūga Province, with magnifient shrine buildings and vast estates. It was also involved in a protracted conflict with [[Tsuma Shrine]], the [[Sōja shrine]] of the province. The details of this conflict are unknown as all of the ancient records have been destroyed. By the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] the Tsuno Shrine was regarded as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hyūga Province. It was rebuilt by the local warlord [[:en:Itō Yoshisuke|Itō Yoshisuke]] in 1549; in 1578, during a conflict between [[:en:Ōtomo Sōrin|Ōtomo Sōrin]] and the [[:en:Shimazu Yoshihisa|Shimazu Yoshihisa]], the shrine was destroyed by fire, and the shrine buildings, shrine treasures, and ancient documents were all destroyed. The shrine never recovered, and by 1675, traveller's accounts stated that it was a small, unattended shrine. The shrine was restored in its current form by Akizuki Tanemasa, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Takanabe Domain|Takanabe Domain]], and in 1701, estates worth 20 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'' were donated for its upkeep. Successive ''daimyō'' of Takanabe supported the shrine through the end of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 3rd Rank |国幣小社|Kokuhei Shosha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] in 1871.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. in 1934, the area of the shrine was expanded and improved as part of the "celebrations of the 2600th anniversary of the founding of Japan" project sponsored by the government. The main shrine building was rebuilt in 2007. The shrine is located 25 minutes on foot or five minutes by car from [[:en:Tsuno Station|Tsuno Station]] on the [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]] [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Gallery== File:Tsuno-jinja haiden.JPG|Heiden File:Tsuno-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den File:Tsuno-jinja kusu.JPG|''[[:en:Camphora officinarum|Camphora officinarum]]'', (Tsuno town Natural Monument) File:Tsuno-jinja kitaootorii.JPG|North Torii ==See also== *[[:en:List of Shinto shrines|List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[:en:Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society.
